Indiana property tax is assessed and collected at the local level, and owners can appeal an assessment.

What the official sources say

  • A taxpayer appeals an assessment by filing Form 130 with the assessing official; deadline is June 15 of the assessment year if the Form 11 notice was mailed before May 1, otherwise June 15 of the year the tax bill is mailed. (DLGF Fact Sheet - Assessment Appeals; source)
  • After a Form 130 filing, the assessing official schedules a preliminary informal meeting, then reports to the county PTABOA, which must hold a hearing within 180 days of filing. (DLGF Fact Sheet - Assessment Appeals (IC 6-1.1-15-1.2); source)

  • Assessed value is meant to reflect the price that would induce the owner to sell and a buyer to purchase, reflecting current use. (DLGF Fact Sheet - Assessment Appeals; source)
  • Redemption of property sold at tax sale requires 110% of the minimum bid if redeemed within six months, or 115% if redeemed after six months but within one year of sale. (IC 6-1.1-25-2(b); source)

What the official sources say

  • For assessment dates after Dec 31, 2024, the homestead standard deduction is $48,000 in 2025, $40,000 in 2026, $30,000 in 2027, $20,000 in 2028 (text continues for later years). (IC 6-1.1-12-37; source)
  • For assessment dates before Jan 1, 2025 the deduction was the lesser of 60% of assessed value or $48,000. (IC 6-1.1-12-37; source)
  • To get a new homestead deduction a taxpayer applies to the county auditor; applications filed before the annual deadline apply to the next tax bill (example given: complete by Jan 15, 2026 for 2025 pay 2026). (DLGF: Deductions and Credits; source)

How much is the Indiana homestead deduction, and is it shrinking?

The standard homestead deduction is dropping every year until it reaches zero, so the amount you get depends on the assessment year. Senate Enrolled Act 1 of 2025 replaced the old formula, which was the lesser of 60 percent of assessed value or $48,000, with a fixed schedule that applies retroactively to January 1, 2025.

Assessment dateStandard deduction
Before Jan. 1, 2025Lesser of 60% of assessed value or $48,000
2025$48,000
2026$40,000
2027$30,000
2028$20,000
2029$10,000
2030 and later$0

A shrinking standard deduction does not mean the total relief disappears. The state added a supplemental deduction and a credit to carry more of the load, which the next section explains.

What is the supplemental homestead deduction and the homestead credit?

The supplemental deduction takes a percentage of whatever value is left after the standard deduction, and that percentage rises each year. It applies to taxes first due and payable after December 31, 2025. It cannot exceed 75 percent of the property's gross assessed value.

Tax yearPercentage of value after standard deduction
2026 taxes40%
202746%
202852%
202957%
203062%
2031 and later66.7%

Here is the arithmetic for a house with a gross assessed value of $200,000 on 2026 taxes. The standard deduction is $48,000, which leaves $152,000. Forty percent of that is $60,800, so the two deductions together remove $108,800. This is an illustration of the formula, not a prediction for your bill.

There is also a supplemental homestead credit for anyone who receives the standard deduction. The credit is the lesser of 10 percent of the homestead's tax liability or $300, it needs no application, and taxes approved by voters in a referendum are left out of the calculation. For 2026 the state applies it after the property tax cap credit and before the over 65 circuit breaker credit.

Who qualifies for the homestead deduction in Indiana?

The person claiming it must use the property as a principal place of residence in Indiana and must hold an interest in it on the assessment date. Under IC 6-1.1-12-37 the interest can take several forms:

  • Ownership by the individual.
  • A recorded contract that makes the buyer responsible for the property taxes and obligates the owner to convey title when the contract is complete.
  • Occupancy as a tenant-stockholder of a cooperative housing corporation.
  • A home held in a trust, when the occupant is a person described in section 17.9, such as someone with a beneficial interest in the trust.

The contract purchaser line matters to anyone who sold a house on a land contract. If the contract is recorded and the buyer pays the taxes, the buyer may claim the deduction on the house while the seller still holds title.

A new definition arrives with House Enrolled Act 1210, effective July 1, 2026. It places in the statute the phrase "an individual's true, fixed, permanent home to which the individual has the intention of returning after an absence."

What counts as the homestead

The deduction covers one house and one garage, plus up to one acre immediately around the dwelling. It can also reach decks, patios, gazebos, pools, one additional yard structure and one additional residential building that is not used as an investment or rental property. Land and buildings beyond that are treated as ordinary residential property and capped at 2 percent instead of 1 percent.

In general a person cannot hold the deduction on two different properties in the same year.

How and when do you apply for the homestead deduction?

You apply by filing a certified statement with the county auditor, and the first filing is the only one you normally make. The Department of Local Government Finance (DLGF) says reapplication is needed only if the property is sold or the title changes.

The deadline needs a careful check. The 2024 text of the statute says the statement must be dated in the preceding calendar year and filed on or before January 5 of the year the taxes are first due. DLGF's own deductions page gives an example with a completion date of January 15, 2026 for the 2025 tax year paid in 2026. Because the two sources differ, call your county auditor and ask which date they enforce before you rely on either one.

  • DLGF offers a Homestead Deduction Form and a separate Change of Use form for people whose use of the property changes.
  • The statement lists the applicant and spouse by name, with the last five digits of each Social Security number or an allowed substitute.
  • The sales disclosure form filed when a house sells can also serve as an application for deductions such as the homestead deduction, so a buyer can use that form to apply.

What happens to the homestead deduction when you sell the house?

The deduction does not move to the buyer on its own. Since reapplication is needed when a property is sold or the title changes, the new owner has to file a fresh statement, and until then the property may be billed without the benefit.

The 1 percent circuit breaker cap makes this more than paperwork. DLGF's fact sheet says the 1 percent cap applies only to homestead property that receives the standard deduction. Take a home assessed at $100,000 with a calculated bill of $2,100. A 1 percent cap holds the bill to $1,000 and the county auditor applies a $1,100 credit. Without the deduction, the 1 percent cap does not apply.

Duties for the seller who moved out

A person who stops being eligible must tell the auditor within 60 days. Starting July 1, 2026, failing to do that while still claiming the deduction makes the person liable for the extra tax plus a civil penalty of 10 percent of the additional taxes. The word in the statute changed from "may" to "shall."

The auditor also has a stronger duty. If a property was ineligible in any year within three years of the tax due date, the auditor shall issue a notice of taxes, interest and penalties, and the notice adds a 10 percent penalty on the total tax bill calculated as if the deduction had not been applied. A vacant inherited house that still carries a deceased owner's deduction is worth a call to the auditor before you list.

Which other credits and deductions follow the owner?

Several senior, disability and veteran benefits changed under the 2025 and 2026 laws, and most are credits that need a separate application by January 15. They stack with each other and with the homestead deduction.

BenefitAmountMain condition
Over 65 creditUp to $150Age 65 by Dec. 31 of the prior year; adjusted gross income of $60,000 (single) or $70,000 (joint)
Over 65 circuit breaker creditVaries by billSame income limits, up from $30,000 and $40,000; $240,000 value limit removed
Blind or disabled creditUp to $125No income limit; principal residence
Veteran credit, age 62 and up$250Disability of 10% or more
Veteran credit, service-connected$350Disability of 10% or more; war-time service
Totally disabled veteran deduction100% of assessed valuePrincipal residence; one year of Indiana residency

From 2026 an over 65 claimant must live on the property, although a nursing home or hospital stay does not disqualify. A credit larger than the year's tax liability does not carry forward or refund.

Owners of rental houses get something too. Residential, long-term care and agricultural property in the 2 percent class receives a deduction applied automatically, set at 6 percent of assessed value for the 2025 assessment and rising to 33.4 percent from the 2030 assessment onward.

Is there a separate homestead protection from creditors in Indiana?

Yes, but it is a different rule. Indiana Code 34-55-10-2(c)(1) exempts real estate or personal property used as the debtor's or a dependent's residence from creditors, up to a dollar limit set by the statute.

Joint debtors can each use that exemption for property held as tenants by the entirety. Under subsection (c)(5), any interest a debtor has in entireties property is exempt, though the exemption does not apply to a debt that the debtor and the debtor's spouse owe together. The dollar amounts are adjusted over time and the sources we read gave different current figures, so confirm the present amount with an Indiana attorney before relying on it in a sale that involves a judgment or bankruptcy.

This protection does not lower a property tax bill, and the tax deduction does not shield a house from a judgment.

More questions about Indiana Homestead Exemption

Does the homestead deduction go away when I sell my Indiana house?

Yes, it ends for you as the owner. DLGF says reapplication is needed when a property is sold or the title changes, so the buyer must file their own statement with the county auditor if they will live there.

What is the Indiana homestead deduction in 2026?

The standard deduction is $40,000 for the 2026 assessment date, down from $48,000 for 2025. A supplemental deduction of 40 percent of the remaining value applies to 2026 taxes, with a cap of 75 percent of gross assessed value.

When is the deadline to file for the homestead deduction?

The statute text we read says January 5 of the year taxes are first due, while DLGF's page gives a January 15, 2026 example. Ask your county auditor which date applies, since the two sources differ.

Can I claim the homestead deduction on a house I am buying on a land contract?

Possibly. Indiana Code allows a contract purchaser to qualify when the contract is recorded, makes the buyer responsible for the property taxes, and obligates the owner to convey title when the contract is complete. The house must also be the buyer's principal residence.

What happens if I keep the deduction after I move out?

You must notify the county auditor within 60 days of becoming ineligible. From July 1, 2026, failing to do so makes you liable for additional taxes plus a 10 percent civil penalty on the extra tax, and the auditor must send a notice for any ineligible year within three years of the due date.

Do landlords get a homestead deduction on rentals?

No. A rental is not a principal place of residence for the owner. Residential property in the 2 percent class gets a separate automatic deduction under the 2025 law and is capped at 2 percent instead of 1 percent.

Indiana Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling

What the official sources say

  • Indiana repealed its inheritance tax in 2013; it applied to those dying on or before Dec 31, 2012 (IC 6-4-1). (Indiana DOR: Inheritance Tax Information; source)
  • No inheritance tax returns for Indiana residents or nonresidents should be prepared or filed after October 5, 2023. (Indiana DOR: Inheritance Tax Information (IC 34-11-1-2); source)

Does Indiana tax estates or inheritances today?

Indiana does not collect an inheritance tax now. The Department of Revenue says the tax applied to people who died on or before December 31, 2012, and the legislature repealed it in 2013.

The Department's page adds two practical points. It says no Indiana inheritance tax returns for residents or nonresidents should be prepared or filed after October 5, 2023, and it states that the inheritance tax forms have been retired. For questions, the Inheritance Tax Division can be reached at 317-232-2154 on weekdays from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Eastern.

The page does not discuss real estate transfers, so it does not tell you what a title company will ask for on a particular deed. Questions about a specific gain go to a tax professional or attorney.

Why does the Indiana Code still mention the old inheritance tax?

Section 6-4.1-4-0.5 of the Indiana Code still refers to the exemptions in the repealed chapter 6-4.1-3 when it allows an affidavit showing that no tax is due.

The same section says a terminated lien can reattach if the Department obtains an order that inheritance tax is owed. If you are handling a very old death in the family, a title search may turn up this language, and an attorney can tell you whether it affects the file.

What about the federal estate tax?

The federal estate tax is a separate system run by the IRS, and it reaches only very large estates. The IRS filing threshold table lists $13,990,000 for 2025 and $15,000,000 for 2026, measured on the gross estate plus adjusted taxable gifts.

The IRS also notes that, since 2011, the estate of a decedent survived by a spouse can elect to pass unused exemption to the spouse, and the election is made on a timely filed estate tax return.

In the IRS wording, a return is required when the gross estate, increased by adjusted taxable gifts and the specific gift tax exemption, exceeds the filing threshold for the year of death. The year of death controls, so a 2025 death uses the 2025 figure even if the house sells in 2026.

TaxStatusSource
Indiana inheritance taxRepealed in 2013; applied to deaths through December 31, 2012Indiana DOR
Indiana inheritance tax returnsNone to be filed after October 5, 2023Indiana DOR
Federal estate tax filing threshold, 2025$13,990,000IRS
Federal estate tax filing threshold, 2026$15,000,000IRS

How does an inherited house get taxed when the heirs sell it?

An heir who sells an inherited house is taxed on gain measured from the value at death, not from what the original owner paid. IRS Publication 551 says the basis of inherited property is its fair market value at the date of the individual's death, or its value on the alternate valuation date if the personal representative chooses that option.

The publication notes one exception for appreciated property that the heir or the heir's spouse gave to the decedent within one year before death. In that case the basis is the decedent's adjusted basis just before death.

  • Ask for the appraisal or the estate's valuation of the house.
  • Keep records of repairs and carrying costs after death.
  • Remember that Indiana adds its flat individual rate on income the federal return reports, as covered on our Indiana capital gains page.

When can heirs skip full probate in Indiana?

For deaths after June 30, 2022, Indiana lets a fiduciary close a small estate without notice to creditors when the gross probate estate, less liens and encumbrances, is within $100,000 plus administration costs and reasonable funeral expenses. Indiana Code section 29-1-8-3 sets that limit.

When the estate includes real property, subsection (c) allows an affidavit to be recorded with the recorder in the county where the land sits. The affidavit must include:

  • The legal description of the property
  • The threshold amount that applies to the date of death
  • The name of each person entitled to an interest and the share each receives, divided or undivided
  • A statement explaining how each share was determined

A related section, 29-1-8-1, lets distributees collect personal property by affidavit 45 days after death if no personal representative has been requested anywhere. That section covers items such as bank funds, vehicles and securities rather than land.

What does unsupervised administration mean for a house sale?

Larger estates go through a personal representative, and heirs can ask the court to let the estate be administered without court supervision. Under Indiana Code 29-1-7.5-1, the decedent's heirs at law, the legatees and devisees, or the personal representative may petition for that authority.

After the petition, the clerk issues a notice and the petitioner serves it on the decedent's known creditors. That statute section does not say whether a representative can sell real estate without an order, so confirm the representative's sale powers with a probate attorney or the clerk of the county where the case is filed.

Indiana has 92 counties, and Howard County, as one example, lists five courts: a Circuit Court and Superior Courts I through IV. Ask the clerk of the county where the case is filed how that court handles estate filings.

What costs keep running while an estate holds a house?

Property tax continues to be billed whether or not the owner has died. For 2026 the installments are due May 11 and November 10, and the state charges 5 percent for payment within 30 days of the due date on a parcel with no back taxes, rising to 10 percent of the unpaid tax after that.

Indiana bills a year behind, so a spring bill after a death often reflects the prior year's ownership. The Howard County Auditor's instructions say a homestead application is renewed only when a property is sold, the title changes or a contract is paid off, so heirs who take title should check their deduction status with the county.

What should heirs gather before listing or selling?

Heirs move faster when the paperwork is in order. A short list covers most of it:

  • A certified death certificate and a copy of the will, if there is one
  • Letters from the court, or the affidavit described above if the estate qualifies
  • The deed, the parcel number and the latest property tax bill
  • The date-of-death value, which becomes the starting basis
  • A list of everyone entitled to a share, since the recorded affidavit names each person and each share

Consult an Indiana probate attorney before signing a deed, because the right route depends on the size of the estate and who holds legal authority.

More questions about Indiana Estate and Inheritance Tax

Does Indiana have an estate tax?

The Indiana Department of Revenue describes only the inheritance tax, which was repealed in 2013 and applied to deaths through December 31, 2012. The federal estate tax is separate and has a 2026 filing threshold of $15,000,000.

Do heirs pay Indiana inheritance tax on a house?

No. The Department says no Indiana inheritance tax returns should be prepared or filed after October 5, 2023, and the inheritance tax forms have been retired.

Does an inherited house get a stepped-up basis?

Generally yes. Under IRS Publication 551 the basis is the fair market value at the date of death, or the alternate valuation date if the personal representative elects it. A gift to the decedent within one year of death is an exception.

How much can an Indiana estate hold and still use the small estate process?

For deaths after June 30, 2022, the limit in section 29-1-8-3 is $100,000 of gross probate estate less liens and encumbrances, plus administration costs and reasonable funeral expenses. The affidavit for real property is recorded with the county recorder.

How long must heirs wait to use the small estate affidavit for personal property?

Forty-five days after the death, and only if no application for a personal representative is pending or granted anywhere. Section 29-1-8-1 sets that rule.

Do property taxes stop when the owner dies?

No. Bills continue on the May and November schedule, and late payments carry 5 percent and then 10 percent charges under the state schedule.

What the official sources say

  • If a tenant fails to pay rent when due, landlord may terminate the lease on not less than 10 days notice unless parties agreed otherwise or the tenant pays in full before the notice period expires. (IC 32-31-1-6; source)
  • A tenancy at will may be ended by one month written notice; a general tenancy with the landlord's consent is month-to-month. (IC 32-31-1-1, 1-2; source)
Selling in Indiana?

Get My Cash Offer →

How does an eviction start in Indiana?

An Indiana eviction begins with a written notice, and the length depends on why the landlord wants possession. For unpaid rent, Indiana Code 32-31-1-6 lets the landlord end the lease on at least ten days' notice, unless the parties agreed otherwise. If the tenant pays the full rent before the notice period runs out, the termination does not go forward.

Indiana Legal Help describes the same ten-day notice as the standard step for nonpayment or another lease violation, and says a landlord cannot end the lease if the rent is paid during those ten days.

Notices under the first seven sections of the chapter can be served three ways under section 32-31-1-9:

  • On the tenant directly
  • On a person living at the property, with the contents explained to that person, if the tenant cannot be found
  • By attaching a copy to a conspicuous part of the premises when no one is there

Which notice period fits which kind of tenancy?

The notice depends on the kind of tenancy, and some situations need no notice at all. Section 32-31-1-8 lists six cases where notice is not required, including a lease for a set period, a contract that states when the tenancy ends, a tenant at will who commits waste and a tenant at sufferance.

SituationWhat the code saysSection
Rent unpaidAt least 10 days' notice, cured if rent is paid in full first32-31-1-6
Tenant at will commits waste, or tenant at sufferanceNo notice required32-31-1-8
Fixed term or stated end dateNo notice required32-31-1-8
No landlord-tenant relationshipNo notice required32-31-1-8

Chapter 32-31-1 also has separate sections on how estates at will and year-to-year tenancies are determined and how notice ends them (32-31-1-1 through 1-5). Read your lease first, since it sets the term that decides which rule applies.

What happens once the case reaches court?

Indiana eviction cases usually run in two parts: a possession hearing first, then a damages hearing that may be held later. At the possession hearing the court decides who should live in the rental unit under the lease. The damages hearing decides whether either side owes money for rent, utilities or repairs.

Indiana Legal Help describes two possession outcomes:

  • Final possession, which is the usual result for unpaid rent, with a move-out date typically two to three weeks away
  • Immediate possession, where the landlord pays money into court to be held in case the tenant later wins, and the tenant can post the same amount to stay until the damages hearing

The most a person can win in small claims court is $10,000, so a tenant who misses the damages hearing can face a judgment up to that amount. A party who does not appear can lose by default, and Indiana Legal Help warns that missed hearings can block a tenant from sealing an old eviction later.

Chapter 32-31-6 of the code also covers emergency possessory orders. Its section titles include small claims jurisdiction, emergency hearings, waste and criminal activity.

Can a landlord change the locks or shut off utilities?

No. Section 32-31-5-6 says a landlord may not deny or interfere with a tenant's access to or possession of the dwelling unless a court order allows it. That covers changing locks and removing doors, windows, fixtures or appliances.

The same section bars cutting off or reducing electricity, gas, water or other essential services, with exceptions for an emergency, good faith repairs or necessary construction. A landlord must give reasonable written or oral notice before entering and may enter only at reasonable times. A tenant may not unreasonably refuse entry for listed purposes such as inspections, repairs or showings.

That last point matters for a landlord who wants to sell, because showings are one of the listed reasons for entry. The section also does not apply to a unit that has truly been abandoned, which requires that the tenant has failed to pay or offer rent and that a reasonable person would conclude possession was surrendered.

Does selling a rented house cancel the lease?

No. Section 32-31-1-10 says a landlord's conveyance of the property or any interest in it is valid without the tenant's attornment. It also says that if the tenant pays rent to the landlord before the tenant receives notice of the conveyance, that payment is good against the new owner.

Chapter 32-31-3 on security deposits has a section titled "Sale of Property; Liability for Deposits; Exceptions" (32-31-3-19), so read it or ask an attorney how the deposit passes at closing. Separately, section 32-31-3-12 requires the landlord to deliver an itemized written notice and the deposit balance within 45 days after the rental agreement ends. The landlord has no liability under the chapter until the tenant supplies a written mailing address.

Allowed deductions are unpaid rent, damages from the tenant's violation of law or the lease, and unpaid utility or sewer charges the lease requires the tenant to pay. A landlord who does not comply can owe the full deposit plus reasonable attorney's fees.

Do Indiana cities set their own landlord rules?

Generally not. Under section 32-31-1-20, local governments may not control rents on private property or regulate the landlord-tenant relationship without state authorization. The list of barred topics includes tenant screening, security deposits, rental applications, lease terms, required disclosures, the rights of parties under a lease and landlord fees.

Any local rule that breaks this section is void and unenforceable. The exception covers private property that receives government funds or benefits to offer reduced rents to low or moderate income tenants.

For a landlord selling in a place like Kokomo or Fort Wayne, the working rules for notices, deposits and eviction therefore come from the state code and the county court, not from a city rent ordinance.

What if the tenant dies or cannot be found?

If a sole-occupant tenant dies, the landlord must follow section 32-31-1-23, which sets up a tenant's representative to collect belongings and the deposit. The representative is chosen in priority order, starting with a person the tenant named in writing to the landlord or in the lease, then an attorney-in-fact, a guardian, an heir, or someone a probate court appoints.

The landlord must give the representative access at a reasonable time to remove personal property, may require an inventory, and must pay the deceased tenant's security deposit and unearned rent. A landlord who follows the section is protected from liability, and a willful violation exposes the landlord to actual damages.

The code also covers an absent, apparently incapacitated sole-occupant tenant with the same steps.

What should a landlord prepare before selling a tenant-occupied Indiana house?

Gather the tenant paperwork before a buyer asks for it. The rules above point to a short list:

  • The lease and any renewal, so the tenancy type and term are clear
  • A rent ledger showing what was paid and when
  • Any notice you served, with proof of how and when it was delivered
  • The security deposit amount, and the tenant's written mailing address if you have one
  • Repair requests and your responses, since Indiana Legal Help lists a recent repair request or code enforcement call as something a tenant may raise in court
  • Court papers if a case is already filed, including hearing dates

If the landlord and tenant can agree on a move-out date, that avoids a hearing altogether. An owner who decides to sell rather than continue a case can still do so, and an attorney can confirm how a pending court order affects the timing.

More questions about Indiana Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

How much notice does an Indiana landlord give for unpaid rent?

At least ten days, under Indiana Code 32-31-1-6. If the tenant pays the full rent before the notice period expires, the lease cannot be terminated for that default.

How long does a tenant have to move after an Indiana judgment?

Indiana Legal Help says a final possession judgment typically sets a move-out date two to three weeks away. The date depends on the court's order in your case.

Can a landlord lock a tenant out in Indiana?

No. Section 32-31-5-6 bars a landlord from denying or interfering with a tenant's access or possession without a judicial order, including by changing locks or cutting off essential utilities.

Does the tenant have to leave if I sell the house?

Not automatically. Section 32-31-1-10 says the landlord's conveyance is valid without the tenant's attornment, which means the sale does not by itself end the lease. A lease ends by its own terms or by proper notice.

When must an Indiana landlord return a security deposit?

Within 45 days after the rental agreement ends, with an itemized written notice of deductions, under section 32-31-3-12. The landlord has no liability until the tenant gives a written mailing address.

Can my city cap rent or add its own eviction rules?

Generally not. Section 32-31-1-20 bars local rent control and local regulation of leases, deposits and landlord fees unless the state authorizes it.

  • An owner may revoke a TOD deed designation by recording before death either a later deed or an acknowledged affidavit revoking or changing it. (IC 32-17-14-11(j); source)

Indiana Transfer on Death Deed Explained FAQ

What is a transfer on death deed?

A recorded deed that names who receives the property when the owner dies. Confirm the Indiana rules with an attorney.

What is a transfer on death deed in Indiana?

It is a deed that passes real estate to a named beneficiary when the owner dies, without a probate transfer of that parcel. Indiana allows it under the Transfer on Death Property Act, IC 32-17-14, and the rules for real estate deeds sit in section 11.

The owner keeps the house for life. The beneficiary has no rights in the property because of the designation until the owner dies, and a sale by the owner ends it.

The statute says the deed works when the owner or the owner's legal representative signs it and it is recorded with the recorder of deeds in the county where the land sits, before the owner dies.

What does a TOD deed need to be valid?

The main requirement is recording during the owner's life. A TOD deed that is not recorded before death is void.

  • No payment is required for the transfer.
  • The deed does not have to be delivered to the beneficiary.
  • The county auditor's endorsement is not needed to record it.
  • The beneficiary can be a revocable or an irrevocable trust.
  • The deed can be worded in substance as a conveyance "TOD to" the beneficiary.

Because delivery is not required, a beneficiary may learn about the deed only after the owner dies. A family that suspects one exists can search the county recorder's records for the parcel.

How does the form of ownership change a TOD deed?

The effect depends on how the owner holds title, and several forms need extra care. Section 11 spells out the outcomes in a list.

Form of ownershipEffect of a TOD deed under IC 32-17-14-11
Tenancy by the entiretyVoid unless the other spouse joins
Joint tenancy with survivorshipSevers the joint tenancy; co-owners become tenants in common
Tenancy in commonThe owner's interest passes to the beneficiary
Life estate measured by the owner's lifeThe conveyance is void

A married couple who hold a house together should not assume one spouse can sign alone. Title questions like these are why a recorded deed is worth reviewing with an attorney.

How do you change or revoke an Indiana TOD deed?

You record a later document in the county before you die. IC 32-17-14-16 says the owner may revoke or change a TOD deed designation by recording either a new deed or an acknowledged affidavit that does so. Unrecorded documents are void.

Several informal steps do not work:

  • Writing on a recorded TOD deed or destroying a copy does not affect the designation.
  • A will or trust cannot revoke or modify a TOD deed.
  • A newer designation replaces an earlier one unless it says otherwise.

Where the owners hold as joint tenants with survivorship, a change needs the agreement of each living owner. For tenants by the entirety, both must agree while both are alive.

What happens if the owner sells the house after signing a TOD deed?

The sale cancels the TOD for that property. Under section 16, transferring the owner's interest during life, whether for payment or not, ends the beneficiary designation for the property. A real estate deed given this way is void unless it is recorded with the county recorder before the owner dies.

So an owner who signed a TOD deed can still sell to a cash buyer. The buyer's title company will search the record, see the TOD deed and confirm the owner's right to convey. The beneficiary has no rights in the home during the owner's lifetime.

This matters for families under pressure. A beneficiary cannot block a sale by the living owner, and an owner who wants to move can sell the house on their own timeline.

Does a TOD deed protect the house from liens and creditors?

No. A beneficiary takes the property subject to the liens and security interests that exist, according to IC 32-17-14-19. A mortgage, a recorded easement or a judgment lien stays on the house after the transfer.

Creditors also keep their rights. IC 32-17-14-29 says the chapter does not limit the rights of an owner's creditors against beneficiaries and other transferees. A beneficiary's liability for creditor claims and statutory allowances is set in IC 32-17-13.

Unpaid property tax is a good example of a lien that follows the house. Our Indiana tax lien guide explains how that lien works. A beneficiary who inherits a house with delinquent tax inherits the tax problem too.

Can a beneficiary sell the house after the owner dies?

Yes, once the beneficiary holds title through the recorded deed, the house is theirs to sell. How long the paperwork takes depends on the county recorder and the title company, and we have not confirmed a statewide step list, so check with both.

Practical points for a beneficiary:

  • Get a certified death certificate.
  • Ask the title company to pull the recorded TOD deed and any later revocation.
  • Check for a mortgage, tax due or liens.
  • Talk to an attorney if a spouse, children or other heirs may have claims. IC 32-17-14-25 deals with the rights of surviving spouses and children.

A house in poor repair can still be sold as is. Cash Home Buyers makes offers on inherited Indiana homes without requiring repairs.

What else does the Transfer on Death Property Act cover?

The act reaches well past deeds. Its section titles show that the same chapter also governs designations on accounts, tangible personal property, and registrations in beneficiary form, so a family may be dealing with several transfers at once.

  • Section 20 requires a beneficiary to survive the owner, and section 22 covers substitution for beneficiaries who do not survive.
  • Section 23 addresses the effect of dissolution or annulment of a marriage.
  • Section 24 addresses fraud, duress, undue influence, mistake and lack of capacity.
  • Section 17 addresses the powers of an attorney in fact, a guardian, a conservator or an agent.
  • Section 32 addresses out-of-state beneficiary designations.

We list these only as headings, since each one has its own conditions. If a family member signed a deed while ill, or a divorce came after the deed was recorded, those sections are the first place for an attorney to look.

When is a TOD deed the wrong tool?

It works best for a single parcel and a clear beneficiary. It fits poorly when the owner has several heirs who may disagree, when the home carries heavy debt, or when the owner wants a trust to manage the property.

  • A beneficiary who dies before the owner raises the survival and substitution rules in sections 20 and 22.
  • Co-owners can undo the intended result by how they hold title.
  • The deed does not remove debts from the property.

An estate planning attorney can compare a TOD deed with a trust or a will for your situation. This page is general information and is not legal advice.

More questions about Indiana Transfer on Death Deed

Does an Indiana TOD deed avoid probate?

For the parcel it covers, yes. The beneficiary takes title through the recorded deed. Other assets in the estate can still need a probate process.

Where do you record an Indiana TOD deed?

With the recorder of deeds in the county where the real estate is located, before the owner's death. A deed recorded after death is void.

Can I cancel a TOD deed by writing a new will?

No. A TOD deed may not be revoked or modified by will or trust. The owner must record a new deed or an acknowledged affidavit before death.

Can the beneficiary stop me from selling my house?

No. Before the owner's death a beneficiary has no rights in the property because of the designation. A sale during life ends the designation for that parcel.

Does the beneficiary have to pay my mortgage?

The beneficiary takes the house subject to existing liens and security interests. The loan stays attached to the property, and lenders keep their rights.

Is the county auditor's signature needed on a TOD deed?

No. IC 32-17-14-11 says the auditor's endorsement is not required to record a TOD deed.

Can a TOD deed name a trust?

Yes. The deed can transfer property to a revocable or an irrevocable trust.

What is a property tax lien in Indiana?

In Indiana, the lien for property tax comes from state law, and it attaches to the land itself. Under IC 6-1.1-22-13, each tract of real property is subject to a lien for the taxes levied on it, plus penalties and costs.

The lien attaches on the assessment date of the year the tax is assessed. A sale or transfer of the property does not remove it. If you sell a house with a year of tax unpaid, the lien stays on the parcel until the tax is paid, which is why the title company deals with it at closing.

The same statute says the lien is superior to all other liens. A mortgage, a judgment lien and a contractor claim all rank behind it. It lasts ten years from May 10 of the year the taxes first became due, and that period can stretch if the county starts enforcement inside it.

When does Indiana property tax become delinquent?

Property tax is delinquent when an installment is not paid by its due date. Under IC 6-1.1-22-9, tax assessed for a year is generally due in two equal installments, May 10 and November 10 of the following year. A due date that falls on a weekend or holiday moves to the next business day, which is why the 2026 dates were May 11 and November 10.

The Department of Local Government Finance posts the current dates on its property tax due dates page. A payment can count as on time if it is received, postmarked, or sent by electronic transfer by the deadline, according to IC 6-1.1-37-10.

Once an installment is late, penalties start right away.

How much are the penalties on late Indiana property tax?

The first penalty is 5 percent of the delinquent amount or 10 percent, depending on how late you are and whether you were already behind. The 5 percent rate applies when a real property installment is paid in full within 30 days of the due date and the owner has no earlier delinquency on that parcel. Any other case is charged 10 percent.

Marion County states the same rule in plain terms on its due dates page: pay within 30 days with no back taxes and the penalty is 5 percent, and after that it rises to 10 percent.

Later years add more. In each following year, an additional 10 percent applies to unpaid tax on the day after each installment due date. The statute applies these later penalties to the unpaid principal only, so the penalty does not compound on earlier penalties.

SituationPenalty under IC 6-1.1-37-10
Paid within 30 days, no earlier delinquency on the parcel5% of the delinquent amount
Any other late payment10% of the amount due
Still unpaid after each later installment dateAdditional 10% on unpaid principal

What happens after property tax stays unpaid?

The county can eventually put the parcel into a tax sale, which is the main route for turning a tax lien into a transfer of ownership. A taxing unit also has the option to sue the person liable for delinquent tax and recover the tax, penalties and collection costs, including reasonable attorney fees and court costs.

Counties handle the steps in order:

  • The county auditor builds a delinquency list and a notice of sale.
  • The county treasurer and auditor ask the court for a judgment and an order of sale.
  • The property is offered at a public auction, subject to redemption.
  • The owner gets a redemption window before a buyer can ask for a tax deed.

The mechanics of the auction and the redemption window are covered on our Indiana tax sale page. This page stays focused on the lien and on getting it cleared.

Can you set up a payment arrangement on delinquent taxes?

Indiana law allows it. The title of IC 6-1.1-24-1.2 covers removing a property from the delinquency list and an arrangement for payment of delinquent taxes. The details differ by county, so ask your treasurer what it will accept.

Marion County lists a tax sale payment plan and partial payments as separate topics on its Stop a Tax Sale page. The Treasurer's Office can be reached at (317) 327-4444 or mytaxes@indy.gov. A homeowner behind on a plan should call before a sale date is set, not after.

For a house you are trying to sell, a payment plan has a limit. The lien stays with the property until the tax is paid in full, so a buyer's title company will still ask for a payoff at closing.

Does a state tax warrant create a lien on an Indiana house?

Yes, an unpaid state tax can become a lien on real estate in the county where the warrant is recorded. This is a different lien from the property tax lien. After a demand notice goes unanswered for 20 days, the Department of State Revenue can issue a tax warrant, and a 10 percent collection fee is added to the unpaid tax, according to IC 6-8.1-8-2.

The clerk of the circuit court records the warrant as a judgment against the taxpayer, and that judgment creates a state lien on the taxpayer's interest in real and personal property in the county. A filed judgment is valid for 10 years and can be renewed for further 10 year periods.

FeatureProperty tax lienState tax warrant lien
SourceIC 6-1.1-22-13IC 6-8.1-8-2
AttachesOn the assessment date, to that tractWhen the clerk records the warrant as a judgment
LengthTen years from May 10 of the year taxes first became due10 years, renewable
PrioritySuperior to all other liensAttaches in the county where it is recorded

A taxpayer can ask for a release once the debt is satisfied, and the department must release a warrant issued in error. Ask your title company to run a search so any warrant shows up before you list.

What is the vacant and abandoned property rule?

Some delinquent parcels are not offered in a regular tax sale at all, and the owner has no redemption right. Under IC 6-1.1-24-1.5, a county, city or town executive can certify a delinquent property that a court or hearing authority found vacant or abandoned. The auditor then sells it by auction, and the owner has no right to redeem after the sale date.

The minimum bid on those parcels equals the property's share of the county's actual sale costs, not the full tax debt. A vacant house with years of unpaid tax is the situation this rule targets.

  • The tax must be delinquent from the prior year's fall installment or earlier.
  • A court or hearing authority must find the property vacant or abandoned.
  • The auditor publishes the sale notice at least 30 days before the sale.

How does Marion County handle tax liens in Indianapolis?

Marion County states it places a tax lien on homes with unpaid property taxes and sells those liens at an online auction. The 2026 online sale was scheduled for October 13 through 16, with registered bidders putting down a $2,500 deposit for the regular portion, according to the Treasurer's bidder page.

To stop a scheduled sale, an owner pays all unpaid taxes, penalties and special assessments, solid waste and stormwater fees, and a $325 tax sale administration fee. The 2026 deadline was October 8 at 4:30 p.m., and payment is limited to cash, certified check, cashier's check or money order.

Marion County Treasurer: City-County Building, 200 E. Washington St., Suite 1001, Indianapolis, IN 46204. Auditor: Suite W-125, phone 317.327.4646.

How do sellers clear a tax lien before closing?

The usual route is to pay the lien from the sale proceeds at closing. The title company orders a payoff from the county treasurer and wires it, so the seller does not need cash up front.

  • Order a current tax bill and a payoff figure that includes penalties.
  • Check for any state tax warrant filed against the owner's name.
  • Confirm whether the parcel is on a delinquency list or has a sale date.
  • If a sale date is near, ask the treasurer for the cutoff time and accepted payment forms.

Cash Home Buyers can buy a house that has these liens and coordinate with the title company so unpaid tax comes out of the proceeds. A seller can request an offer without making repairs first.

More questions about Indiana Tax Liens and Delinquent Property Tax

How long does a property tax lien last in Indiana?

Ten years from May 10 of the year the taxes first became due. If the county starts enforcement inside that period, the deadline can extend as needed to finish it.

Can I sell my house with a tax lien in Indiana?

Yes. The lien follows the property, so the unpaid tax is paid from the sale proceeds at closing. A title company confirms the payoff amount before the deed is recorded.

Does a tax lien rank ahead of my mortgage?

Yes. IC 6-1.1-22-13 makes the property tax lien superior to all other liens, so it is paid before a mortgage in a forced sale.

What is the penalty for paying Indiana property tax late?

Five percent if you pay within 30 days and have no earlier delinquency on the parcel. Ten percent in any other case, and an extra 10 percent on unpaid principal after each later due date.

Is a state income tax warrant the same as a property tax lien?

No. A tax warrant is issued by the Department of State Revenue and recorded with the circuit court clerk as a judgment. It creates a lien on the taxpayer's real and personal property in that county.

Who do I call in Indianapolis about delinquent property tax?

Call the Marion County Treasurer's Office at (317) 327-4444 for balances and payments. The Auditor's Office at 317.327.4646 handles tax sale questions.

Does Indiana have its own capital gains tax on a house sale?

The Department of Revenue's rate page lists one individual rate and no separate capital gains rate for a house. The statute starts with federal adjusted gross income as defined in Section 62 of the Internal Revenue Code and then applies Indiana's own additions and subtractions, so a taxable gain that lands on your federal return flows into the state calculation.

The Department of Revenue lists the individual adjusted gross income tax rate at 2.95 percent for 2026 and 2.90 percent for 2027. That one rate applies to the whole income figure, gain included.

Counties add their own income tax on top. The Department's Departmental Notice #1, effective for periods beginning on or after October 1, 2026, lists Howard County at 0.0235, or 2.35 percent. For withholding, the notice ties a taxpayer to a county by residence on January 1, and the Department says county rates can be adjusted in January and October.

What does the federal home sale exclusion cover?

For most sellers, the federal exclusion decides whether any gain reaches the state calculation at all. The IRS says you can exclude up to $250,000 of gain, or $500,000 if you file jointly with a spouse, when you sell your main home.

The tests in IRS Topic 701 are specific:

  • You or your spouse owned the home for at least 24 months of the last 5 years.
  • The home was your residence for at least 24 months of the last 5 years, and both spouses must meet this test on a joint return.
  • You must meet both tests during the 5 years ending on the sale date, though the two 24-month periods can fall in different stretches.
  • You cannot use the exclusion if you excluded gain from another home sale within the previous two years.

If you receive a Form 1099-S, you report the sale even when the gain is fully excludable. When the exclusion does not cover everything, Schedule D and Form 8949 come into play. A person on qualified official extended duty can elect to suspend the five-year period for up to ten years.

How are gains above the exclusion taxed federally?

A gain on property held more than one year is long term, and the IRS taxes it at 0, 15 or 20 percent depending on taxable income. Gain on property held one year or less is short term and taxed as ordinary income.

The 2025 thresholds shown on the IRS capital gains page are below, and they change each year, so confirm the current ones before filing.

Filing status0 percent up to15 percent up to
Single$48,350$533,400
Married filing jointly$96,700$600,050
Head of household$64,750$566,700

The same page says 20 percent applies above the 15 percent range, that unrecaptured section 1250 gain has a 25 percent maximum rate, and that people with significant investment income may owe the net investment income tax. It also states that a loss on the sale of a personal home is not deductible.

Which Indiana adjustments matter to someone selling a house?

The most useful one is a subtraction for property taxes paid on a principal residence, up to $2,500 ($1,250 for separate filers). It appears in the statute's list of subtractions from federal income, alongside Social Security benefits and certain military income.

The statute also lists additions, such as state income taxes deducted on the federal return and certain bonus depreciation and Section 179 amounts. Owners who depreciated a rental house should go through that list with a preparer.

Because Justia's copy of the code may lag behind the legislature, check the current Indiana tax booklet before relying on a dollar limit. The Department says individual filers find current county rates in the IT-40 booklet.

What if the house was inherited?

Gain on an inherited house is measured from a stepped-up starting value, which usually means much less taxable gain than the original purchase price would suggest. IRS Publication 551 says the basis of inherited property is its fair market value at the date of death, or the value on the alternate valuation date if the estate's personal representative elects that.

One exception applies: if you or your spouse gave appreciated property to the decedent within a year before death, your basis is the decedent's adjusted basis immediately before death. Keep the appraisal or the estate's valuation, since it becomes your cost figure when you report the sale.

Our separate Indiana estate and inheritance tax page covers the repealed state inheritance tax and how probate affects who can sign the deed.

What about a rental house or an investment property in Indiana?

The home sale exclusion applies to a main home, so a rental usually produces a taxable gain. The IRS says gain from real property that is unrecaptured section 1250 gain is taxed at a maximum of 25 percent.

Indiana then applies its rate to the federal income figure after the state's own modifications. Your total bill also depends on the federal bracket, the county rate and whether you qualify for the exclusion.

If a tenant occupies the house, the landlord's selling options and notice duties are separate questions, covered on our Indiana eviction process page.

How can you estimate the tax before you sell?

Start with arithmetic you can check yourself. Suppose a single filer has a $60,000 taxable gain above the exclusion, purely as an illustration. At the 2026 state rate of 2.95 percent, that gain adds $1,770 of Indiana tax, and the county rate in the Department's notice applies on top for a resident of the county it lists.

Gather these items before you ask a preparer to run numbers:

  • The purchase closing statement and receipts for capital improvements
  • The dates you moved in and moved out, to test the 24-month rules
  • Any prior home sale where you used the exclusion
  • The date of death and valuation, if you inherited
  • Records of depreciation, if the house was ever a rental
  • Your county of residence on January 1

What Indiana facts frame a home sale here?

Indiana has 92 counties and, per the 2020 census, 6,785,528 residents, with Indianapolis the largest city at 887,642. Manufacturing employs about 17 percent of non-farm workers, the highest share of any state.

Indiana taxes the gain through its individual adjusted gross income tax, which the Department of Revenue sets at 2.95 percent for 2026 and 2.90 percent for 2027. Your county adds its own income tax rate on top.

Does Indiana tax the portion of gain that the federal exclusion covers?

Indiana begins with federal adjusted gross income, so gain you exclude federally does not appear in that starting figure. The statute's later modifications can still change the result, so a preparer should check your return.

Up to $250,000, or $500,000 on a joint return, if you meet the ownership and residence tests in 24 of the 60 months before the sale and have not used the exclusion within two years.

No. Under IRS Publication 551 the basis is generally the fair market value at the date of death, so gain is measured from that value. Gifts to the decedent within one year of death are an exception.

Departmental Notice #1 lists Howard County at 0.0235, or 2.35 percent, for periods beginning on or after October 1, 2026. County rates can change in January and October.

Yes, if you receive a Form 1099-S. The IRS says to report the sale even when the gain is excludable. Schedule D and Form 8949 are used when you cannot exclude all of the gain.

How does an Indiana tax sale work?

An Indiana tax sale is a public auction of a delinquent parcel, and the sale is subject to redemption. The county auditor publishes a notice listing the eligible properties, and the auditor and treasurer then apply to the court for a judgment and an order of sale, as laid out in IC 6-1.1-24-2.

The notice names the owner (or at least one owner), gives the parcel key number and street address, and states the sale place, dates and times. If the sale is online, it must say so and explain how to join. An owner who wants to contest the judgment must file a defense with the court and serve the auditor and treasurer before the earliest application date in the notice, and the court sets a hearing at least seven days before the advertised sale.

Buyers at the sale are not buying the house outright. They are buying the county's lien, and the owner can still pay to get the property back during the redemption period.

What is the minimum bid at an Indiana tax sale?

The minimum bid is the total of the delinquent tax and the costs of running the sale, and no parcel sells for less. The statute lists five pieces that make up that figure.

  • Delinquent taxes and special assessments.
  • Taxes and assessments due in the sale year, whether or not yet delinquent.
  • Penalties on the delinquencies.
  • An auditor fee equal to the greater of $25 or postage and publication costs, plus other actual costs tied to the sale.
  • Unpaid costs from a prior tax sale.

A buyer can bid above the minimum. The extra money is called the overbid, and it matters to the owner because it can become surplus, as explained below.

How long do you have to redeem a house after a tax sale?

An owner usually has one year from the date of sale to redeem, and 120 days if the property was sold to a qualified purchasing agency. That rule is in IC 6-1.1-25-4.

Other situations change the clock:

  • Property on the county's vacant and abandoned list has no right to redeem.
  • If the county acquires a lien that is not sold as a certificate, redemption runs 120 days from the day the lien is acquired.
  • A parcel that was offered but did not sell gets 120 days from the end of the sale.

Marion County repeats the two main periods on its redemption amount page: one year from the sale date for a sold parcel and 120 days for a parcel that was offered but did not sell.

The treasurer and an owner may also agree in writing to extend redemption by one year, as long as the owner pays the full redemption amount before the extended period ends. If the owner breaks that agreement, the treasurer can end it with 30 days' written notice.

How much does it cost to redeem?

The redemption amount is built from several parts, set out in IC 6-1.1-25-2. The base is 110 percent of the minimum bid if you redeem within six months of the sale, or 115 percent if you redeem after six months but within the year.

ComponentRule
Base amount110% of minimum bid within 6 months; 115% after that
OverbidAmount the price exceeded the minimum bid, plus 5% per year (sales after June 30, 2014)
Taxes the buyer paid after the saleReimbursed with 5% per year interest (sales after June 30, 2014)
Certified costsAttorney fees, notice costs and title search costs, certified to the auditor
New delinquenciesTaxes, penalties and fees that became delinquent after the sale

Because the base percentage jumps after six months, redeeming early is cheaper.

What does a tax deed do to the owner's title?

If nobody redeems, the buyer can petition for a tax deed, and that deed ends the owner's interest. Under IC 6-1.1-25-4, the deed conveys a fee simple absolute, free of most liens, with exceptions such as recorded easements and governmental police powers.

The deed has a deadline too. The auditor cannot issue or record it unless, within 150 days after the court hearing that grants the buyer's petition, the court order and sales disclosure form are filed, recording fees are paid, and all outstanding property taxes are paid.

An owner who sits on a house after a sale has a short and costly path left. The practical choice is to redeem or sell before the deed issues.

Do you get money back if the house sells above the minimum bid?

Possibly. If a parcel sells for more than the minimum bid and is not redeemed, the former owner of record may have a right to the surplus, as noted in the sale notice requirements and in IC 6-1.1-24-7.

The buyer's payment goes first to the taxes, assessments, penalties and costs, then to other delinquent taxes, and any remainder goes into a tax sale surplus fund.

  • The owner of record may file a verified claim for the surplus.
  • If the auditor and treasurer approve, the auditor issues a warrant for the amount due.
  • Surplus not claimed within three years after receipt goes to the county general fund.

Claims through a contract holder, executor, attorney in fact or guardian are routed through the court, and a court may direct payment only within three years after the sale. Indiana also limits agreements for recovering surplus money, and the attorney general enforces those limits.

How does Marion County run its tax sale?

Marion County runs an online tax lien sale each year, with the 2026 sale scheduled for October 13 through 16 from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. Its bidder page says the non-profit portion runs first, then the regular portion, and that parcels are auctioned in numeric order without a break between townships.

Bidders for the regular portion post a $2,500 deposit, and registration closed October 7 at 3 p.m. New bidders without evidence of credit from a bank were approved for $100,000 as individuals or $250,000 as companies.

Marion is a consolidated city county, so the surplus rule differs from other counties. The treasurer may pay taxes that come due during the redemption period out of the surplus held in the owner's name.

Owners can check whether a parcel sold with the sold parcel finder. Tax sale questions go to the Auditor at MCATaxSale@indy.gov.

How can you stop a tax sale in Marion County?

You stop it by paying everything owed before the cutoff. For 2026, that meant all unpaid taxes, penalties and special assessments, solid waste and stormwater fees, and a $325 administration fee by October 8 at 4:30 p.m., per the Treasurer's Stop a Tax Sale page.

On the day of the public auction, the Treasurer collects payment after 8 a.m. in room 1001 of the City-County Building. Personal and business checks are refused.

Selling the house before the auction is another way out. A buyer's closing pays the tax from the proceeds, and the parcel never reaches the sale. A seller who has already received notice should call (317) 327-4444 to confirm what is owed.

What should an Indiana seller weigh before the sale date?

The decision comes down to timing, money and the condition of the house.

  • Check the redemption figure first, because it rises after six months.
  • Ask whether the parcel is on the vacant and abandoned list, where no redemption exists.
  • Find out whether the home has equity above the tax debt. If it does, selling protects that equity.
  • Keep copies of every notice you receive.

Cash Home Buyers buys houses as-is, including ones facing a tax sale. We can walk through the numbers with you and the title company.

More questions about Indiana Tax Sales

Can I still redeem my Indiana house after the tax sale?

Yes, in most cases. You generally have one year from the date of sale, or 120 days if the property was sold to a qualified purchasing agency. Parcels on the vacant and abandoned list have no redemption right.

What is the redemption percentage in Indiana?

It is 110 percent of the minimum bid within six months of the sale and 115 percent after six months but within the year. Other costs and interest are added on top.

Who buys at an Indiana tax sale?

Registered bidders. In Marion County for 2026, regular bidders posted a $2,500 deposit and registered by October 7.

Can I get the surplus if my house sold above the minimum bid?

Possibly. If the property is not redeemed, the owner of record may file a verified claim. Unclaimed surplus goes to the county general fund after three years.

How do I stop a Marion County tax sale?

Pay the full balance, including penalties, fees and the $325 administration fee, by the posted deadline. The Treasurer takes cash, certified checks, cashier's checks or money orders only.

Can I sell my house before it goes to tax sale?

Yes. A sale that closes before the auction lets the title company pay the tax debt from the proceeds. Confirm the payoff amount and the sale date with the county first.

Indiana Land Contracts: Seller Rules FAQ

What is a land contract?

A contract where the buyer pays over time while the seller keeps title until a set point.

What is a land contract in Indiana, and how common is it?

A land contract is a financing arrangement in which the seller finances the purchase directly and the buyer pays in installments until the balance is repaid. In most cases the seller keeps the deed until the last payment, so the buyer lives in the house and carries repairs, maintenance and property taxes without holding legal title.

Indiana uses them more than its size suggests. Pew counted 31,431 recorded land contracts from 2005 to 2024, the sixth-most of any state, while Indiana ranked 17th in population in 2024. About 90 percent financed residential property. Recordings peaked at 3,521 in 2010, fell to a low of 612 in 2017 and reached 1,098 in 2024.

The counties with the highest land contract shares of home sales were Jennings at 5.3 percent, Howard at 4.9, Elkhart at 4.3 and Washington at 4.1. Pew also found that corporate entities made up 30 percent of land contract sellers, and in Marion County nearly half of land contracts involved companies.

Does Indiana have one law for land contracts?

No, Indiana has no comprehensive land contract statute. Pew's 2026 fact sheet says the rules are spread across the First Lien Mortgage Lending Act, the Home Loan Practices Act and the 1973 Indiana Supreme Court case Skendzel v. Marshall.

A 2021 National Consumer Law Center summary, which Pew hosts, fills in what those laws do for a land installment contract:

  • A creditor that regularly extends first lien credit, including through land installment contracts, must be licensed by the state.
  • Covered creditors may not engage in unfair or deceptive practices, must give a timely payoff on request and may not charge a prepayment penalty.
  • Creditors that regularly make land installment contracts fall under the Home Loan Practices Act ban on deceptive and misleading acts, IC 24-9-3-7.

Pew adds that Indiana sets no limits on interest rates, fees or contract terms for these deals, and a contract does not have to be publicly recorded. That gap is why two contracts on similar houses can read very differently.

What must an Indiana land contract seller disclose?

A seller under a land contract must tell the buyer about any encumbrance on the property that affects title, and must do it in writing by certified mail with return receipt requested. IC 24-9-3-7(d) names tax liens, foreclosure actions and judgments as examples.

The timing depends on when the encumbrance appears. If it already exists at or before signing, the notice is due no later than signing. If it arises afterward, the notice is due within ten business days after it is created. A seller who misses the deadline commits a prohibited act under the same statute.

The residential disclosure form is a second layer. Indiana Code 32-21-5-1 says the seller-disclosure chapter reaches installment sales contracts, as well as sales, exchanges and lease-purchase deals, for residential real estate with no more than four dwelling units. The owner must complete and sign the form and give it to the buyer before accepting an offer, and an owner is not liable for an error that was outside the owner's actual knowledge, unless the owner was negligent in obtaining or passing on the information.

Transfers by a fiduciary of an estate, trust or guardianship, and transfers by a lender after foreclosure, sit outside that chapter. A seller in one of those roles should not assume the form applies.

Can an Indiana seller keep the buyer's payments after a default?

Not automatically. Indiana courts treat many land contracts like mortgages, so a seller who wants out after a default is often steered toward foreclosure instead of forfeiture. The key case is Skendzel v. Marshall, decided by the Indiana Supreme Court in 1973.

In that case the parties signed a $36,000 contract in December 1958. The buyers had paid $21,000 and still owed $15,000 when they stopped paying after January 1965. The sellers tried to enforce a clause letting them keep every payment and retake the house. The Supreme Court reversed and sent the case back with instructions to foreclose the vendor's lien under the mortgage foreclosure statute.

The court's reasoning has stayed influential:

  • The retained title works like a lien that secures the unpaid balance.
  • Forfeiture is not banned outright, but it should be used "with great caution and only where fairness and justice demand it."
  • Judicial foreclosure, which includes a six-month redemption period, protects the seller's security while preserving the buyer's substantial rights.

Morris v. Weigle (1978) applied the idea. A buyer had paid about 29.7 percent of the price and had not abandoned the farm, so the court rejected the seller's claim to keep $24,722.97 and ordered foreclosure. The decisions describe forfeiture as fitting an abandoning buyer, or a buyer who paid very little, has little equity and stays in possession while the seller covers taxes, insurance and upkeep.

How do contract terms change those protections in practice?

Written terms can narrow the buyer's cushion even when the case law is favorable. Pew found that in Marion County many contracts limit foreclosure to buyers who have paid at least 15 percent to 60 percent of the balance.

A Fair Housing Center of Central Indiana review of about 40 Marion County contracts, as reported by WFYI, found default terms that let sellers file for eviction without notice. A mortgage lender would have to go through foreclosure, which gives the homeowner a chance to pay the debt and keep the house. Some people were reportedly removed without any eviction or foreclosure filing.

WFYI also reported that Indiana lawmakers have considered requiring land contracts to be filed with the county clerk, but that bill never reached the governor. Illinois, by comparison, requires sellers to record within ten business days of the sale. For a seller in Indiana the lack of a filing duty means the file in your own drawer, and the payment history in it, may be the best proof of what happened.

What should you check before selling a house tied to a land contract?

Start by identifying who holds title today and what the contract still requires. Because the seller keeps the deed in most land contracts, ownership of the house and the right to live in it sit with different people until the last payment.

  • The payment record. Total paid and balance owed show how much equity the buyer holds, which matters under Skendzel.
  • Default language. Look for any percentage threshold that limits foreclosure, and for clauses that allow eviction without notice.
  • Liens and judgments. A seller owes the buyer certified mail notice of any encumbrance that affects title.
  • Property taxes. Confirm who has been paying them. A buyer under a recorded contract who pays the taxes may be the one claiming the homestead deduction.
  • Recording. A recorded instrument must be acknowledged by a notarial officer and must state the grantee's mailing address, which must be a street or rural route address under IC 32-21-2-3.

Equity in the house, an unpaid balance and a buyer still living there all affect what a purchaser can do. Gather the contract, the payment history, any default notices and a title report, and take them to an Indiana attorney before signing anything new.

This page is general information, so the contract's effect on a sale is a question for your own lawyer.

More questions about Indiana Land Contracts and Contracts for Deed

Is a land contract legal in Indiana?

Yes. Indiana allows land contracts, though there is no single statute that governs them. The rules come from the First Lien Mortgage Lending Act, the Home Loan Practices Act and case law such as Skendzel v. Marshall.

Do land contracts have to be recorded in Indiana?

No. Pew reports that Indiana contracts do not have to be publicly recorded, which is why the total number in the state is unknown. Lawmakers have considered a filing requirement, but that bill did not reach the governor.

Can a seller evict a land contract buyer in Indiana?

Sometimes, but the route depends on the buyer's equity and the contract terms. Under Skendzel, courts often require foreclosure instead of forfeiture when a buyer has paid a substantial share of the price.

What does a land contract seller have to tell the buyer?

The seller must send written notice by certified mail, return receipt requested, of any encumbrance that affects title. It is due by signing if the encumbrance already exists, or within ten business days if it appears later.

Does the Indiana seller disclosure form apply to land contracts?

Yes, for residential property with no more than four dwelling units. IC 32-21-5-1 covers installment sales contracts, so the owner completes and signs the form before accepting an offer.

What is the difference between forfeiture and foreclosure on a land contract?

Forfeiture lets the seller keep the payments and retake the house. Foreclosure runs through the court, keeps the buyer's equity in play and includes a six-month redemption period as described in Skendzel.
